newsitem.title: USA: Iraq oil exports to peak March around 618,000 bpd.
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil exports to peak March around 618,000 bpd.

text.p: Iraqi oil exports will peak in the late February, early March period at a rate of around 618,000 barrels per day (bpd), according to sources at the United Nations.

The flow of Iraqi oil under the "oil-for-food" deal with the U.N. is skewed toward the latter part of the first 90-day period which ends in early March, though the U.N. overseers charged with monitoring the deal have so far approved deals for only 293,000 bpd for the second 90-day period which ends in early June.

The deal has proved difficult to manage because of the unexpectedly strong interest shown by a wide range of oil companies wanting to buy Iraqi oil, as well as stronger-than-expected oil prices, according to oil traders and diplomats.

U.N. overseers report that Iraq had exported 10.7 million barrels of oil in a total of nine cargoes worth about $237 million up to January 3, making the rate 428,000 bpd since the deal began on December 10, according to sources.

Another 13.9 million barrels were scheduled to be loaded in January, bringing the rate up above 496,000 bpd. But some 40 percent of the first 90 days' oil will be loaded in the last 30 days, according to the overseers' report.

The U.N. has approved contracts for a total of around 46.38 million barrels for the first 90 day period, or slightly over 515,300 bpd. The total includes three contracts approved Tuesday, including those for Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp, for a total of 30,000 bpd.
The average price for Iraqi oil in the first 25 days was $22.15 a barrel which, if sustained for the first 90 days, would bring the amount raised to $1.027 billion.

Under the terms of the U.N. deal, Iraq is allowed to export $1 billion worth of oil over 90 days and up to $2 billion over 180 days. U.N. overseers see some of the revenue from the first 90 days' shipments falling due in the second 90-day period.

Nevertheless, to keep within the allowed amount, Iraq asked six contractors to voluntarily cut back on the amounts they originally signed for, and oil traders say the companies asked to cut were chosen on "political" grounds.

Iraqi State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) executives "say the oil ministry asked them to cut back on countries that were not so supportive to them" during the long negotiating process with the U.N. last year, said one oil trader with an Iraqi contract.

Chevron and Texaco were each asked to cut their originally contracted amounts in half to 10,000 bpd over six months, though Coastal Corp and Mobil Corp weren't asked to cut their contracts for 60,000 bpd and 20,000 bpd, respectively.

Both Italian concerns with contracts, Agip and Oil Energy were asked to halve their amounts to 10,000 bpd and 3,333 bpd, and Mitsubishi Corp had to push one of its two cargoes into the second 90-day period, effectively reducing its contracted amount to 20,000 bpd.
-- ((Tony McAuley/Patrick Connole, New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1620))
